senses.gloss: Worried and unhappy.
examples: She had a *troubled* look on her face.
He was deeply *troubled* by what he'd heard.
I could tell something was wrong — he sounded *troubled*.

senses.gloss: Full of problems, conflict or trouble.
examples: The company has had a *troubled* history.
They grew up in a *troubled* neighborhood.
It was the most *troubled* year of her life.

senses.gloss: Causing trouble, difficulty or annoyance.
examples: A *troublesome* cough kept her up all night.
The most *troublesome* part of the job is the paperwork.
Those old pipes have always been *troublesome*.

contrast: *Troubling* news makes you worried; a *troubled* person already is worried.

senses.gloss: Making people worried or uneasy.
examples: The report raises some *troubling* questions.
What he said was deeply *troubling*.
The most *troubling* part is that nobody noticed.

senses.gloss: Quick to argue or fight; aggressively unfriendly.
examples: He turned *truculent* as soon as the subject came up.
A *truculent* teenager slouched in the doorway.
Her tone grew more *truculent* with every question.

senses.gloss: Completely loyal to a person, a party or a team.
examples: He's a *true-blue* Yankees fan.
She stayed *true-blue* through the whole scandal.
They want a *true-blue* conservative on the ticket.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a true-false question*

senses.gloss: Of a test question that you answer by marking it either true or false.
examples: The quiz is twenty *true-false* questions.
I'd rather have a *true-false* test than an essay.
Each *true-false* item is worth one point.

contrast: Hyphenated before a noun (*a true-to-life story*), usually written open after a verb (*the story is true to life*).

senses.gloss: Showing people and events the way they really are.
examples: It's a *true-to-life* portrait of a small town.
The dialogue is remarkably *true-to-life*.
Her novel is more *true-to-life* than the movie version.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *trumped-up charges*
form: compound — from the phrasal verb *trump up* 'invent'

senses.gloss: Invented in order to accuse someone; not real.
examples: He was jailed on *trumped-up* charges.
The whole case rests on *trumped-up* evidence.
They fired her for some *trumped-up* reason about expenses.

senses.gloss: Cut short; made shorter by cutting off the end.
examples: We played a *truncated* version of the game.
The file names come out *truncated* on that screen.
Rain gave us a *truncated* season.

contrast: *Trusted* means other people trust you; *trusting* means you trust other people easily.

senses.gloss: That people rely on and believe.
examples: She's his most *trusted* adviser.
Get your news from a *trusted* source.
Only a few *trusted* employees have the key.

contrast: A *trusting* child believes everyone; a *trusted* friend is one everyone believes.

senses.gloss: Ready to believe that other people are honest and mean no harm.
examples: He's too *trusting* for his own good.
She gave me a *trusting* look and handed over the money.
Kids are more *trusting* than adults.

senses.gloss: Honest and reliable, so that people can trust you.
examples: She needed a *trustworthy* babysitter.
Is that website *trustworthy*?
He's the most *trustworthy* person I know.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *my trusty pocketknife*
contrast: Half-joking, and used of old reliable objects; a person is *trustworthy*. Also a noun in prisons (*a trusty*).

senses.gloss: Old and reliable — said of a thing you have depended on for years.
examples: He fixed the fence with his *trusty* hammer.
I took notes in my *trusty* little notebook.
She drove out there in the *trusty* old pickup.

contrast: A person is *truthful*; a statement is *true*.

senses.gloss: Telling the truth; not lying.
examples: Just be *truthful* with me.
She wasn't *truthful* about where she'd been.

senses.gloss: Giving a true account of how something really is.
examples: It's a *truthful* description of what the job is like.
The movie is more *truthful* than the book.

contrast: Nothing to do with *trying* to do something — the adjective means 'hard to put up with'.

senses.gloss: Hard to bear; testing your patience.
examples: It's been a *trying* week.
Those last few months were *trying* for everyone.
She stayed calm under the most *trying* conditions.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *tsarist Russia*
contrast: Also spelled *czarist*, which is the commoner spelling in American books.

senses.gloss: Of the emperors who ruled Russia before 1917.
examples: The building dates from *tsarist* times.
*Tsarist* Russia had no parliament until 1906.
He collects *tsarist* coins and medals.

contrast: Informal and a little rude; *heavy* or *overweight* is the polite word.

senses.gloss: Short and fat, in a mild, informal way.
examples: A *tubby* little dog waddled past.
He's gotten *tubbier* since he stopped running.
I felt *tubby* in that sweater.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a Tudor house*
contrast: Also the family name of the English kings and queens from 1485 to 1603.

senses.gloss: Of the Tudor kings and queens of England, or built in the dark-beamed style of that time.
examples: They bought a *Tudor* house with dark beams across the front.
The class is reading a play from the *Tudor* period.
*Tudor* England was smaller than you'd think.

senses.gloss: Full of noise, confusion and sudden change.
examples: It was a *tumultuous* decade in American politics.
Their marriage was short and *tumultuous*.

senses.gloss: Very loud and excited — of a crowd or its noise.
examples: She got a *tumultuous* welcome at the airport.
The speech ended to *tumultuous* applause.

contrast: Also a noun for a person from Tunisia: *she's a Tunisian*, *the Tunisians*.

senses.gloss: From Tunisia, or having to do with Tunisia.
examples: We ate at a *Tunisian* place near the station.
The *Tunisian* coast is full of small white towns.
Her husband is *Tunisian*.

senses.gloss: Full of trouble, conflict and sudden change.
examples: He grew up during a *turbulent* period in the country's history.
Their relationship has been *turbulent* from the start.

senses.gloss: Of air or water: moving violently and unevenly.
examples: The plane hit *turbulent* air over the mountains.
The river is *turbulent* for a few days after a storm.

senses.gloss: Of writing or speech: heavy, pompous and hard to get through.
examples: The report is two hundred pages of *turgid* prose.
His speeches are *turgid* and far too long.

senses.gloss: Swollen with liquid.
examples: The plant cells were *turgid* with water.
The bite left the skin red and *turgid*.

senses.gloss: From Tuscany in Italy, or done in the style of that region.
examples: We rented a *Tuscan* farmhouse for a week.
The kitchen is done in a *Tuscan* style.
He ordered the *Tuscan* white bean soup.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *twin sisters*, *twin engines*
contrast: Much commoner as a noun (*she has a twin*). Before a noun it is the adjective.

senses.gloss: Born at the same time from the same mother.
examples: Her *twin* brothers are in the same class.
The *twin* girls still dress alike.

senses.gloss: Being one of two matching things.
examples: The room has two *twin* beds.
The plane has *twin* engines.
The *twin* towers of the cathedral are visible from the highway.

contrast: Also a noun in *in the twinkling of an eye* 'in an instant'.

senses.gloss: Shining with small, quick changes in brightness.
examples: *Twinkling* lights hung across the porch.
She looked up at him with *twinkling* eyes.
From up here the whole valley is *twinkling*.

senses.gloss: Bent or turned out of its proper shape.
examples: The frame was *twisted* in the crash.
A *twisted* piece of wire held the gate shut.

senses.gloss: Strange and unpleasant in a cruel way.
examples: That's a *twisted* thing to say.
He has a *twisted* sense of humor.
The plot gets more *twisted* with every episode.

senses.gloss: Having many bends.
examples: It's a narrow, *twisty* road up the mountain.
The trail gets *twistier* near the top.

senses.gloss: Of a story: full of unexpected turns.
examples: It's a *twisty* thriller that keeps you guessing.
The plot is *twisty* but it holds together.

senses.gloss: Flat — having length and width but no depth.
examples: A drawing is *two-dimensional*; a sculpture isn't.
The map gives you a *two-dimensional* version of a round earth.

senses.gloss: Of a character in a book or movie: shallow, with no real inner life.
examples: The villain is completely *two-dimensional*.
Even the minor characters are less *two-dimensional* than in the first book.

senses.gloss: Saying one thing to someone's face and another behind their back.
examples: I didn't realize how *two-faced* he was.
She called her boss a *two-faced* liar.
That was a *two-faced* thing to do.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a two-lane road*

senses.gloss: Of a road: having one lane of traffic in each direction.
examples: It's a *two-lane* highway the whole way there.
They're finally widening the *two-lane* bridge.
We took the old *two-lane* road along the river.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the two-party system*

senses.gloss: Involving or controlled by two main political parties.
examples: The United States has a *two-party* system.
Third parties rarely break the *two-party* hold on Congress.
He's arguing for an end to *two-party* politics.

ru: состоящий из двух предметов; раздельный (о купальнике)
position: attributive only — before a noun: *a two-piece suit*
contrast: Also a noun for a swimsuit: *she wore a two-piece*.

senses.gloss: Made of two separate matching pieces.
examples: He wore a gray *two-piece* suit.
She bought a *two-piece* swimsuit.
The desk comes as a *two-piece* set.

ru: состоящий из двух направлений (о плане, атаке)
position: attributive only — before a noun: *a two-pronged approach*

senses.gloss: Having two separate parts that work at the same time.
examples: They took a *two-pronged* approach to the problem.
It was a *two-pronged* attack, from the north and from the west.
The bill is a *two-pronged* attempt to cut costs and raise revenue.

senses.gloss: Having two sides that are both used or printed on.
examples: Use the *two-sided* setting to save paper.
The sign is *two-sided*, so you can read it from either direction.

senses.gloss: Having two points of view that both deserve a hearing.
examples: Every argument is *two-sided*.
It's a *two-sided* story, and we've heard only one half.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a two-timing husband*
form: compound — from the verb *two-time* 'cheat on a partner'

senses.gloss: Cheating on a wife, husband or partner by secretly seeing someone else.
examples: She threw the *two-timing* jerk out of the house.
It's a country song about a *two-timing* boyfriend.
He got a reputation as a *two-timing* husband.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *a two-way street*
contrast: *A two-way street* is also an idiom for something both sides have to do: *respect is a two-way street*.

senses.gloss: Working or moving in both directions.
examples: It's a *two-way* street, so watch for oncoming cars.
The crew talked on *two-way* radios.

senses.gloss: Involving two people or sides equally.
examples: Trust is a *two-way* deal.
It has to be a *two-way* conversation, not a lecture.

contrast: Also an adverb, and that use is commoner: *sales rose twofold*.

senses.gloss: Having two parts, or twice as large.
examples: The problem is *twofold*: no money and no time.
We saw a *twofold* increase in traffic.
Her purpose in coming was *twofold*.

contrast: Nearly always in *typographical error* — in everyday speech people just say *typo*.

senses.gloss: Having to do with how text is set and printed.
examples: There's a *typographical* error on the cover.
The only mistakes left are *typographical*.
He made a few *typographical* changes to the layout.

senses.gloss: Using power over other people in a cruel and unfair way.
examples: They finally got rid of a *tyrannical* boss.
The regime grew more *tyrannical* every year.
His father was *tyrannical* about bedtimes.

senses.gloss: Curved like the letter U.
examples: The desks were set up in a *U-shaped* arrangement.
A *U-shaped* valley was carved out by a glacier.
The driveway is *U-shaped*, so you never have to back up.

senses.gloss: Found everywhere; seeming to be in every place at once.
examples: Cell phones are *ubiquitous* now.
Those *ubiquitous* orange cones mean road work ahead.
Coffee shops are more *ubiquitous* here than anywhere else I've lived.

contrast: Also a noun for a person from Uganda: *he's a Ugandan*.

senses.gloss: From Uganda, or having to do with Uganda.
examples: He teaches at a *Ugandan* university.
The *Ugandan* team won the relay.
Her parents are *Ugandan*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *an ulterior motive*
contrast: Almost always in *ulterior motive* — a hidden reason behind a friendly-looking act.

senses.gloss: Hidden, and different from the reason a person gives.
examples: I think he has an *ulterior* motive for helping.
She offered with no *ulterior* purpose at all.
There's always some *ulterior* reason with that family.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *the ultimate goal*
contrast: Also a noun in *the ultimate in* + noun: *the ultimate in comfort*.

senses.gloss: Final; coming at the end of a process.
examples: The *ultimate* decision is hers.
Our *ultimate* goal is to get everyone housed.

senses.gloss: The best or greatest of its kind.
examples: It's the *ultimate* road trip.
That's the *ultimate* compliment, coming from her.

contrast: Also a noun for a person: *the ultraconservatives in the party*.

senses.gloss: Far to the right politically, or strongly opposed to any change.
examples: He writes for an *ultraconservative* magazine.
Her views on schooling are *ultraconservative*.
The district keeps electing *ultraconservative* candidates.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *ultraviolet light*
contrast: Shortened to *UV* in everyday talk: *UV rays*, *UV index*.

senses.gloss: Of light waves just beyond violet, which the eye cannot see but which burn skin.
examples: Sunscreen blocks *ultraviolet* rays.
They check the bills under an *ultraviolet* lamp.
*Ultraviolet* light kills bacteria on the surface.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *umpteen times*
contrast: Informal, and always a vague 'a lot' — you never say how many, and you cannot count them.

senses.gloss: A large but uncounted number of.
examples: I've told you *umpteen* times to close the door.
There are *umpteen* ways to do this.
She has *umpteen* cousins in Ohio.

contrast: Nearly always in *for the umpteenth time*, said in exasperation.

senses.gloss: Coming after a large, uncounted number of others.
examples: For the *umpteenth* time, no.
This is the *umpteenth* meeting about the same thing.
He was watching the *umpteenth* rerun of that show.

contrast: A political insult, not a neutral word: it means 'against American values', not 'not from America'.

senses.gloss: Against what the speaker takes to be American values.
examples: He called the protest *un-American*.
Censorship is *un-American*, they argued.
Nothing is more *un-American* than telling people how to pray.

senses.gloss: Not at all embarrassed or ashamed, where most people would be.
examples: She's an *unabashed* fan of bad movies.
He was completely *unabashed* about asking for more money.
There was *unabashed* joy on their faces.

position: both — often after a verb: *the rain continued unabated*

senses.gloss: Going on at full strength, without getting any weaker.
examples: The rain continued *unabated* all night.
Demand for tickets was *unabated*.
*Unabated* construction has changed the whole neighborhood.

senses.gloss: Printed or recorded complete, with nothing cut out.
examples: I listened to the *unabridged* audiobook.
It's the *unabridged* edition, all nine hundred pages.
The text on this page is *unabridged*.

senses.gloss: So bad or wrong that you cannot allow it.
examples: That kind of language is *unacceptable* here.
The delay is *unacceptable* to our customers.
They sent back an *unacceptable* offer.

senses.gloss: With nobody going along.
examples: *Unaccompanied* minors have to check in at the desk.
Children under twelve may not ride *unaccompanied*.

senses.gloss: Of music: sung or played with no instruments behind it.
examples: She sang the last verse *unaccompanied*.
It's a piece for *unaccompanied* cello.

senses.gloss: Impossible to explain.
examples: For some *unaccountable* reason, he turned around and left.
There was an *unaccountable* delay at the border.

senses.gloss: Not having to answer to anyone for what you do.
examples: The agency is *unaccountable* to voters.
Power that is *unaccountable* gets abused.

senses.gloss: Not used to something.
examples: He was *unaccustomed* to the heat.
She's *unaccustomed* to being told no.

senses.gloss: Not usual; not what that person normally does.
examples: He spoke with *unaccustomed* warmth.
There was an *unaccustomed* quiet in the house.

senses.gloss: Impossible to reach or carry out.
examples: The deadline was *unachievable* from the start.
They set an *unachievable* target and then blamed the staff.
Nothing here is *unachievable* if we start now.

senses.gloss: Not admitted, not noticed, or not thanked for.
examples: Her work went *unacknowledged* for years.
There's an *unacknowledged* rule about where people sit.
My email is still *unacknowledged*.

position: both — often after a verb: *the problem went unaddressed*

senses.gloss: Of a problem or a question: not dealt with.
examples: The safety issues went *unaddressed* for months.
Several *unaddressed* complaints are still in the file.
That part of the question is *unaddressed* in the report.

senses.gloss: Plain, with nothing added for decoration.
examples: The room was white and *unadorned*.
He gave the *unadorned* facts and sat down.
It's a simple, *unadorned* wooden box.

senses.gloss: Complete, with nothing mixed in — used to make the next word stronger.
examples: That is pure, *unadulterated* nonsense.
The look on his face was *unadulterated* joy.

senses.gloss: Of food or drink: pure, with nothing added to it.
examples: They sell *unadulterated* honey straight from the hive.
The oil is *unadulterated* — nothing in it but olives.

ru: не склонный к риску; пресный, скучный

senses.gloss: Not willing to try new or risky things, and dull as a result.
examples: I'm pretty *unadventurous* when it comes to food.
It was a safe, *unadventurous* choice.
The menu is more *unadventurous* than I expected.

contrast: In the second sense the opposite is *affected* 'putting on an act', not 'influenced'.

senses.gloss: Not changed or harmed by something.
examples: Most of the town was *unaffected* by the flood.
Prices for *unaffected* products stayed the same.

senses.gloss: Natural and sincere, with no show about it.
examples: She has an *unaffected* way of talking to everyone.
His manner is warm and *unaffected*.

senses.gloss: Not belonging to or connected with a particular organization or party.
examples: The clinic is *unaffiliated* with any hospital.
*Unaffiliated* voters can't vote in the primary.
He's registered as *unaffiliated*.

position: predicative only — after a verb: *she seemed unafraid*

senses.gloss: Not frightened.
examples: She walked right up to the dog, completely *unafraid*.
He was *unafraid* of losing the job.
They're *unafraid* to say what they think.

position: both — often after a verb: *he walked unaided*
contrast: Also fixed in *the unaided eye* — without a telescope, microscope or glasses.

senses.gloss: Without help from anyone or anything.
examples: A week later she was walking *unaided*.
The comet is visible to the *unaided* eye.
He finished the puzzle *unaided*.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *unalienable rights*
contrast: *Inalienable* is the ordinary modern word; *unalienable* survives mainly because the Declaration of Independence used it.

senses.gloss: Of a right: that cannot be taken away or given up.
examples: The Declaration speaks of certain *unalienable* rights.
They call free speech an *unalienable* right.
Those are *unalienable* liberties, the judge wrote.

senses.gloss: Exactly as it was before; not changed.
examples: The recipe has come down *unaltered* for a hundred years.
His opinion remains *unaltered*.
They published the *unaltered* transcript.

senses.gloss: Having only one possible meaning; perfectly clear.
examples: The instructions need to be *unambiguous*.
She gave an *unambiguous* no.
The evidence is clear and *unambiguous*.

contrast: The stress falls on the second syllable, and the word starts *yoo-*, not *oo-*.

senses.gloss: Agreed on by everyone, with nobody against it.
examples: The vote was *unanimous*.
The jury reached a *unanimous* verdict.
The committee was *unanimous* in recommending her.

position: both — often after a verb: *he showed up unannounced*

senses.gloss: Happening with no warning that it was coming.
examples: He showed up at the door *unannounced*.
There was an *unannounced* inspection on Tuesday.
She left *unannounced* sometime in the night.

senses.gloss: That cannot be answered.
examples: Kids ask *unanswerable* questions.
Why some people recover and others don't is *unanswerable* right now.

senses.gloss: That cannot be argued against.
examples: The case against him is *unanswerable*.
She made an *unanswerable* argument for waiting.

position: both — often after a verb: *the letter went unanswered*

senses.gloss: That nobody has replied to or explained.
examples: My letter went *unanswered*.
There are still a lot of *unanswered* questions.
The phone rang *unanswered* for a full minute.

senses.gloss: Not expected, and so not planned for.
examples: The trip had a few *unanticipated* expenses.
An *unanticipated* snowstorm closed the airport.
The side effects were entirely *unanticipated*.

senses.gloss: Not sorry, and not pretending to be.
examples: He's completely *unapologetic* about the way he votes.
She wrote an *unapologetic* defense of the program.
The music is loud and *unapologetic*.

senses.gloss: Not attractive or pleasant; not something anyone would want.
examples: Both options are *unappealing*.
Cold eggs make an *unappealing* breakfast.
The idea of another meeting is deeply *unappealing*.

contrast: American spelling is *-izing*; British books write *unappetising*.

senses.gloss: Looking or smelling as though it would not taste good.
examples: The soup looked gray and *unappetizing*.
It was an *unappetizing* pile of something on the plate.
Cafeteria food is famously *unappetizing*.

position: both — often after a verb: *she felt unappreciated*

senses.gloss: Not thanked for or valued as much as deserved.
examples: She quit because she felt *unappreciated*.
His years of work went largely *unappreciated*.
It's an *unappreciated* little museum on a side street.

senses.gloss: Seeming cold or distant, so that people are afraid to start a conversation.
examples: The new manager comes across as *unapproachable*.
He has an *unapproachable* air about him.
She's friendlier than she looks — not *unapproachable* at all.

senses.gloss: Feeling no shame about something other people might think you should.
examples: He's *unashamed* of where he came from.
It was an *unashamed* attempt to get attention.
She's *unashamed* about loving bad TV.

senses.gloss: So strong that it cannot be attacked or argued against.
examples: By halftime they had an *unassailable* lead.
Her reputation was *unassailable*.
The logic of the argument is *unassailable*.

contrast: Praise, not criticism: it means modest, not weak.

senses.gloss: Modest and quiet; not trying to seem important.
examples: He's a quiet, *unassuming* man who happens to run the company.
The restaurant is small and *unassuming*.
She was the most *unassuming* person in the room.

ru: свободный, не состоящий в отношениях; неприкреплённый

senses.gloss: Not married and not in a relationship.
examples: Most of her friends are still *unattached*.
He came to the wedding *unattached*.

senses.gloss: Not joined or connected to anything.
examples: One wire was left *unattached*.
The garage is *unattached* to the house.

senses.gloss: Impossible to reach or get, however hard you try.
examples: The magazines sell an *unattainable* standard of beauty.
For most families that price is simply *unattainable*.
He set himself an *unattainable* goal and then gave up.

position: both — often after a verb: *don't leave bags unattended*

senses.gloss: Left with nobody watching or looking after it.
examples: Do not leave your bags *unattended*.
An *unattended* campfire started the whole thing.
The register was *unattended* for ten minutes.

senses.gloss: Not good-looking.
examples: He's not *unattractive*, just not my type.
It's an *unattractive* building on a beautiful street.

senses.gloss: Not appealing as a choice or an offer.
examples: The terms of the loan are *unattractive*.
Both options look *unattractive* from here.

contrast: American spelling is *-ized*; British books write *unauthorised*.

senses.gloss: Done or made without official permission.
examples: *Unauthorized* vehicles will be towed.
Someone made an *unauthorized* charge on my card.
The biography is *unauthorized*.

senses.gloss: Not able to be had, bought or seen.
examples: That size is *unavailable* right now.
The records are *unavailable* to the public.

senses.gloss: Of a person: not free to talk to or meet.
examples: She was *unavailable* for comment.
He's *unavailable* until Thursday.

senses.gloss: Impossible to prevent or get out of.
examples: A short delay is *unavoidable*.
There were *unavoidable* costs nobody had budgeted for.
The conclusion is *unavoidable*: we need more people.

contrast: The 'mentally ill' sense is old-fashioned and unkind; careful writers avoid it.

senses.gloss: Not giving equal weight to each side; uneven.
examples: The coverage was *unbalanced* — one side got all the airtime.
An *unbalanced* diet will catch up with you.

senses.gloss: Mentally disturbed.
examples: The letters came from someone clearly *unbalanced*.
His lawyer argued that he was mentally *unbalanced*.

senses.gloss: Too painful, unpleasant or annoying to put up with.
examples: The heat was *unbearable* by noon.
He's *unbearable* when he loses.
The waiting was the most *unbearable* part.

senses.gloss: Impossible to defeat.
examples: At home, that team is *unbeatable*.
She had an *unbeatable* record that season.

senses.gloss: Better than anything else — of a price, an offer or a spot.
examples: They advertise *unbeatable* prices on tires.
The location is *unbeatable*.

contrast: *Unbeaten* is a fact — nobody has beaten them yet; *unbeatable* is a judgment — nobody can.

senses.gloss: Having lost no games or races so far.
examples: They're *unbeaten* going into the playoffs.
It's the school's first *unbeaten* season in thirty years.
His record in that weight class is still *unbeaten*.

contrast: In the military phrase *conduct unbecoming an officer* it follows the noun and takes no preposition. The older sense 'not flattering' (*an unbecoming hat*) now sounds dated.

senses.gloss: Not suitable for a person in that position; slightly shameful.
examples: That kind of sniping is *unbecoming* in a senator.
He was fired for conduct *unbecoming* a teacher.
There was an *unbecoming* eagerness in the way he agreed.

position: predicative only — almost always in the fixed phrase *unbeknownst to* + person
contrast: Only ever used in *unbeknownst to someone* — you cannot say *an unbeknownst fact*.

senses.gloss: Without a particular person knowing about it.
examples: *Unbeknownst* to his parents, he'd dropped two classes.
The meeting had been moved, *unbeknownst* to half the staff.
She had been paying the bill for years, *unbeknownst* to him.

senses.gloss: So surprising, good or bad that it is hard to take in.
examples: The view from up there is *unbelievable*.
It's *unbelievable* how fast kids grow.
That was the most *unbelievable* finish I've ever seen.

senses.gloss: Too unlikely to be true.
examples: His excuse was frankly *unbelievable*.
The whole story is *unbelievable*.

contrast: American spelling has one *s*: *unbiased*, not *unbiassed*.

senses.gloss: Fair, with no preference for one side over another.
examples: We need an *unbiased* account of what happened.
No news source is completely *unbiased*.
The new study is more *unbiased* than the first one.

senses.gloss: With no mark, fault or stain on it.
examples: He retired with an *unblemished* record.
Her reputation is *unblemished*.
They only sell *unblemished* fruit.

senses.gloss: Staring steadily, without blinking.
examples: The cat watched him with an *unblinking* stare.
Her eyes were wide and *unblinking*.

senses.gloss: Looking straight at something hard or ugly without flinching.
examples: It's an *unblinking* look at life in the camps.
He gave an *unblinking* account of his own mistakes.

position: attributive only — before a noun: *her unborn child*

senses.gloss: Not yet born; still inside the mother.
examples: She worried about her *unborn* baby.
The drug can harm an *unborn* child.
They argue about the rights of *unborn* children.
